quick.summary: How to stop work from getting stuck by making items smaller.
quick.takeaway: Slice the items at the top of your list so they fit the team.

parts.title: Slicing work down

beats.line: The team took one ticket, but it took three weeks. What went wrong?
The piece of work was much too big for them to chew.
Imagine trying to eat an entire birthday cake in one single bite.
I would choke. You have to cut it into slices first.
Exactly. Work is the same. Large items belong at the very bottom.
We call the process of slicing backlog refinement.
Can I just say cutting it down?
Yes. Cutting it down. Only the top items need to be small.
But how do I know if a slice is small enough to start?

parts.cliff: How to size the work just right.

beats.line: It is small enough when the team can finish it in days.
Think of a mailbox. A small envelope drops right in immediately.
But a big package gets stuck, and you have to force it.
Right. The slot is your team capacity. Big boxes need a new plan.
Your top list items must fit the slot. They need clear borders.
So I keep the top items tiny, and the bottom ones huge.
Exactly. Do not waste time cutting a cake you are not eating today.
I only slice the work we are about to pull next.
That keeps the team moving and saves you hours.

quiz.question: When should you slice a massive piece of work into smaller parts?
options: When it moves to the top of your list to be worked on soon.
As soon as the idea is added to the bottom of the list.
After the team has already started working on it.
Only when the management asks for an update.
quiz.explanation: You should only spend time slicing work that is about to happen.

quiz.question: Every item in your backlog must be small and perfectly sliced.
quiz.explanation: Only the top items need to be small. The bottom items should stay large until they are ready to move up.
